preamble: Total assimilation of the coda tap [ɾ] to a following palatal nasal [ɲ], giving a geminate [ɲɲ]. In western Cuban Spanish (the provinces from Pinar del Río to Matanzas and Cienfuegos, including Havana, plus the municipalities of Corralillo and Trinidad), coda /ɾ/ and coda /l/ merge and assimilate to the next consonant. Inside a word Spanish has no /j/ or /ɲ/ after /l/ or /ɾ/, except after a prefix (superyó), so this geminate arises only across word boundaries; Arias (2019) calls [ɟ˺ɟ] and [ɲɲ] "combinaciones exclusivas de la fonética sintáctica". Arias treats [ɲɲ] as /n/ + /ɲ/ and expects ver ñáñigos and ven ñáñigos to sound alike (ve[ɲɲ]áñigos). Guitart (1978, 2004), the only researcher to study these cross-word assimilations systematically, describes [ɟ˺ɟ] and [ɲɲ] (as summarized by Arias 2019). The unassimilated pronunciations remain more common.

languageExamples.context: Word-final, before a word beginning with /ɲ/
